data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism relies on comparing verisimilitude among theories it explicitly acknowledges 'may be false,' claiming the preferred theory has 'highest verisimilitude' and is 'closest to truth so far.' However, Popper's own formal definition of verisimilitude (truth content minus falsity content) was proven defective by Miller and Tichý (1974): under Popper's definition, comparative verisimilitude among false theories is either trivial or undefined. The target's entire defense hinges on ranking theories by truth-likeness while simultaneously conceding they may be false. But the very metric invoked to rank them—verisimilitude—is formally incoherent precisely when applied to false theories. Therefore the claim that the better-corroborated theory is the 'best approximation to the truth' is not merely a pragmatic choice; it invokes a comparative measure that, in the case the target itself identifies as relevant (theories that may be false), cannot deliver the ordering the argument requires. This is a distinct failure from the previously raised induction objection: it concerns not whether the rule smuggles in probabilistic assumptions, but whether the non-probabilistic metric the rule substitutes for probability is formally capable of doing the comparative work the mechanism demands.
